The Stealth Round

Analysing unannounced
equity investments in the UK
funding market

2021

2
An unannounced fundraising is an investment 
completed without any press coverage or 
statement from the recipient company or 
participating funds. A company may choose to 
announce a deal for marketing purposes, raising 
brand awareness to bring in more customers and 
new talent, or to attract investors ahead of their 
next fundraising. Yet almost 70% of all equity 
deals are still kept quiet.
There are numerous reasons why a business 
may decide not to disclose fresh funding: the 
company could be operating in ‘stealth mode’ 
and so wants to stay under the radar; the round 
could be a precursor to a more significant event 
that they don’t want to hint at, such as an IPO; 
the company is hiding a down round—a deal 
in which shares are sold at a lower price than 
before; or they just simply don’t see it as being 
newsworthy or relevant.
But with early-stage startups lacking the 
sophisticated PR departments that bigger 
companies have, it’s often the most exciting 
ventures that don’t announce their deals. These 
businesses also tend to attract smaller round 
sizes, backed by publicity-shy angel investors, 
one of the most active investor types in the UK’s 
high-growth economy. 
With such a large proportion of equity deals 
going unannounced, it’s not surprising that 
40% of UK startups and scaleups have raised a 
silent round. And this includes some of the most 
valuable companies in the country, as 58% of 
active UK unicorns (private companies worth 
over $1b) have secured an unannounced deal—
and for 1 in 3 of them, their very first equity raise 
was not announced.
These unannounced fundraisings, also known 
as ‘stealth rounds’, are integral to understanding 
the UK’s high-growth ecosystem. In this report, 
we’ll explore the key characteristics of these 
unannounced rounds, and compare them to 
deals shared with the public. Plus, we’ll take a 
closer look at four innovative UK businesses that 
have never announced their deals to the public.

Methodology and key terms
Methodology
Data for this report was finalised on 15 September 2021. To be included in our 
analysis, any investment must be:
•	
Some form of equity investment
•	
Secured by a non-listed UK company
•	
Issued between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2020
announced and unannounced fundraisings
An unannounced fundraising is an investment made into a private company that 
is completed without press coverage or a statement from the recipient company 
or funds that made the investment. As we’ll see througout this report, these 
transactions are an integral part of the UK’s high-growth economy.
Beauhurst is the only data provider to have comprehensive and structured 
coverage of unannounced deals in the UK. These are simply investments that are 
not announced to the public.
Using Beauhurst’s proprietary technology, we monitor all SH01s (forms submitted 
when businesses issue new shares) filed to Companies House. Sometimes, these 
filings may not show genuine investment, as with the exercise of employee 
options, restructuring shares to make cap tables tidier or companies paying for 
services in shares instead of cash. Our algorithm sorts through this minefield, 
flagging filings that indicate a genuine investment. Our in-house Data team then 
investigates and verifies if a new investment has been made. 
Unannounced rounds are subject to a time lag because filings don’t have to be 
submitted immediately. For this reason, we normally exclude unannounced 
deals from any temporal analyses. In this case, where unannounced deals are the 
subject of our analysis, we’ve set the upper bound of the deal date to the end of 
2020, to reduce the effect of this lag. Any 2021 filings for deals that were made 
before the start of the year will still be included. 
Key terms
equity fundraising
Equity fundraising refers to the issuance and sale of new shares by a company 
and not merely the sale of existing shares. This is because new shares fund the 
growth and development of a company, while selling existing shares usually 
results in money flowing to the shareholders.
company stage of evolution
We categorise companies into seven stages of evolution (Seed, Venture, Growth, 
Established, Zombie, Exited, Dead), using over 40 proprietary criteria, and taking 
a balanced view with each decision. You can read more about these stages, and 
typical company characteristics in each one, here. 
valuations
An equity raise with a pre-money valuation that is at least 5% lower than the 
recipient company’s previous post-money valuation is classed as a ‘down round’. 
At least 5% higher is classed as an ‘up round’. And between 5% lower and 5% 
higher is classed as a ‘flat round’.
company sector
We tag companies with as many sectors from our proprietary sector matrix as 
appropriate.

4
Key trends
Proportion of deals, by volume, that are announced to the press (2011 – 2020)
Proportion of deals, by value, that are announced to the press (2011 – 2020)
Despite drastic changes in the volume and value of 
equity deals completed since 2011, the proportion 
that go unannounced has remained consistent. On 
average, unannounced deals make up 68% of total 
deals, ranging from a low of 65% to a high of 71%. 
That equates to 32.9k unannounced deals since 
2011, compared with 15.2k that were announced. 
Meanwhile, the proportion of pounds invested 
that go unannounced is far lower. Between 2011 
and 2020, just 30p in every £1 invested into UK 
companies was unannounced. Year to year, this 
figure is also more changeable than the proportion 
of deals that go unannounced, peaking in 2013 (at 
39%) and dropping in 2016 (to 25%). 
Overall, there’s a gentle downward trend in 
the proportion of pounds invested that go 
unannounced, from 33% in 2011 to 26% in 2020. 
This is no doubt due to the rise of megadeals (worth 
£50m+), which are far more likely to be announced. 
In fact, 45 megadeals were secured in 2020 (versus 
just five in 2011), 93% of which were announced.

Indeed, round size seems to have a huge 
impact on whether a deal is announced to the 
public or not. Over the last decade, 76% of 
deals under £500k have gone unannounced, 
compared to just 13% of investments over 
£10m. 
And whilst median deal size for announced 
rounds has risen pretty steadily, to a high of 
£800k in 2019, for unannounced deals, this 
figure is consistently low, between £150k and 
£200k.

Proportion of announced deals by 
ordinal number of the fundraising
Proportion of announced deals by 
company stage of evolution at deal date
As expected, a relatively large proportion 
(76%) of fundraisings secured by seed-
stage startups go unannounced. Still 
early on in their growth journeys, these 
businesses may not yet have the means 
or desire to announce their investment 
rounds, or may still be operating in 
‘stealth mode’ while they focus on 
research and product development.
Whereas, for venture and growth-stage 
companies, the proportion of deals that 
go unannounced stands at 62% and 
54%, respectively. They’re more likely to 
announce new fundraisings as they gain 
more traction, stakeholders, and media 
attention.
Interestingly, established companies 
buck this trend, with 72% of their deals 
going unannounced—whilst these 
businesses tend to have been around 
for many years, they may have only 
recently secured their first round of 
equity investment (unlike earlier-stage 
companies that are likely to have been 
venture-backed from a young age).
First and second-time fundraisings are 
much more likely to go unannounced 
than later rounds, at 71% of deals—
compared to 62% by round five, and just 
46% by the tenth funding round. This 
suggests that companies may hold off on 
announcing deals until they’ve proven 
their worth and have had a chance to put 
the new capital into effect.

A North–South 
Divide 
Fundraisings are less likely to be announced in the 
South than in the North of England, at 76% of deals 
in the South East and 75% of deals in the South 
West—compared with 49% in the North East (the 
only region where more than 50% of rounds are 
announced) and 65% in the North West. Companies 
in Scotland (53%), Wales (54%), and Northern 
Ireland (59%) are also more like to announce 
rounds.
Funding availability may be a factor here—the 
South receives a disproportionately large amount 
of the equity rounds completed in the UK. 
Companies may be more inclined to announce 
investment in areas where it’s less common. 
Funding to the North also has a bigger impact on 
the local economy, and is hence more newsworthy. 
There are also several public funds with a focus on 
the North of England and the devolved nations, 
which have an obligation to announce their deals. 
Key trends
There are several public funds with a 
particular focus on the North of England and 
each of the devolved nations, which have an 
obligation to announce their deals. These funds 
include Scottish Enterprise, the Development 
Bank of Wales, Invest Northern Ireland, and 
Northstar Ventures.

Proportion of announced deals by selected company sectors
Deals secured by life sciences firms are 
proving less likely to go unannounced 
than those in other industries. Whilst 
unannounced deals make up around 
65% of investments into digital security, 
cleantech, and eHealth companies, just 
55% of raises by businesses operating in 
the life sciences sector are kept quiet. 
This figure was even lower in 2020 (51%), 
perhaps due to the added light thrown 
on pharmaceuticals and biotech during 
COVID-19 making it more appealing for 
businesses in these areas to announce 
new deals.  
Even more notable, however, are 
challenger banks—only 47% of 
fundraisings secured by this fintech 
vertical are unannounced. We suspect 
this is a reflection of these new banks—
such as Monzo, Revolut, OakNorth and 
Starling Bank—trying to be more ethical 
and transparent than established firms, 
sharing information on their investments 
and shareholders with customers to gain 
their trust. 
These industry disruptors are also 
frequenters of crowdfunding, whereby 
they raise equity funding from the 
pockets of the public. Advertised across 
various crowdfunding platforms, and 
often oversubscribed, these round types 
are also more likely to be picked up by 
the press, even if the company itself 
hasn’t notified them of the raise.

Whose keeping quiet?
Companies in focus
Despite the trends, not every unannounced deal in the UK is a small, first-time funding 
round, with the biggest unannounced fundraising to date being insurance broker 
Howden Group Holdings’ latest £446m round, secured in September 2020. Other large 
investments that went unannounced include Zopa’s £140m raise in March 2020, Arrival’s 
£134m raise in April 2019, and Metro Bank’s £126m raise in June 2012. 
Meanwhile, many companies never announce their deals to the public. Here are five 
businesses that have chosen to keep the details of every one of their equity rounds under 
wraps.
ClearBank 
ClearBank aims to rectify the inadequacies of the UK’s clearing banks. Its cloud-based 
platform grants access to the UK clearing system through an API, so payments can be 
made in real-time. Unlike other challenger banks, ClearBank has kept each of its five 
equity funding rounds quiet at the time of completion—it’s raised £181m in total. 
Date founded  2015
Headquarters  Bristol
Number of employees  250–499
Roborace 
Roborace has developed its own class of motorsport racing, in which all the participating 
cars are self-driving and electric. This racing class lets brands test out their technology, 
encourages the development of autonomous software, and introduces a new robotics 
accolade. With six unannounced rounds under its belt, Roborace has secured £72.7m.
Date founded  2015
Headquarters  London
Number of employees  25–49
Quotient Sciences 
Quotient Sciences provides accelerated drug development and manufacturing services 
for the pharmaceuticals industry. Since 2011, Quotient Sciences has raised two equity 
funding rounds, both of which went unannounced. The latest of these, totalling £90.5m, 
was secured in October 2019, and took the company’s total funds raised to £107m. 
Date founded 
1990
Headquarters  Nottingham
Number of employees  500–999
Constellation AI 
Constellation AI develops software aimed at improving AI conversational abilities, for 
use in customer service centres. To date, the company has raised £70.5m worth of equity 
investment, across four unannounced funding rounds. Our research indicates the most 
recent of these was a £62.1m round, secured in January 2021.
Date founded  2016
Headquarters  London
Number of employees  25–49
Rekki 
Rekki develops software that enables chefs and suppliers to communicate. The free 
mobile app was designed and created by ex-chefs, ex-suppliers and restauranteurs to 
support independent restaurants’ and the hospitality industry. So far, Rekki has secured 
£47.3m in six fundraising rounds with the most recent round totalling £20.1m in 2019.
Date founded  2016
Headquarters  London
Number of employees  50–99
